title: Field Notes from a Skeptic Who Stayed
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Field notes, three in the morning, because insomnia has apparently become my preferred venue for theology these days.
Narrator: I spent a decade training myself to distrust any claim that couldn't survive a peer review process, and tauhid, admittedly, doesn't submit to journals.
Narrator: [carefully] What kept me tethered wasn't a syllogism that finally silenced my objections. It was noticing how conveniently my doubt arrived whenever obedience grew inconvenient.
Narrator: I'd dressed inconvenience up as intellectual rigor for years, congratulating myself on a skepticism that was, on closer inspection, remarkably selective.
Narrator: [reflective] The turning point wasn't a debate I won. It was a debate I finally admitted I'd been quietly rigging from the outset.
Narrator: Colleagues assume faith and empiricism sit in permanent opposition, as though certainty about causation were something physics itself actually offers anyone.
Narrator: [honestly] It doesn't, not really. Every experiment I run rests on assumptions I cannot ultimately prove, only trust provisionally, the way I now trust considerably larger claims.
Narrator: That's not a knockdown argument for tauhid, I want to be careful here. It's simply an admission that my prior certainty was borrowed, not earned.
Narrator: [gently] What tauhid asked of me wasn't the abandonment of inquiry, but the humility to admit inquiry has a ceiling I kept mistaking for a wall.
Narrator: Behind that ceiling, I've started to suspect, isn't absence at all. It's simply a vantage point mine was never built to reach unaided.
Narrator: [calmly] My mother, who never finished secondary school, arrived at conclusions it took me a doctorate and considerable stubbornness to approach sideways.
Narrator: I used to find that humbling in an uncomfortable way. Now I mostly just find it funny, in the way true things often are.
Narrator: [encouraging] Tomorrow I'll run the same experiments, cite the same rigorous standards, distrust the same shoddy methodology I've always distrusted on principle.
Narrator: But I'll do it, finally, as someone who suspects the universe was authored rather than merely occurring, and finds that suspicion oddly steadying.
Narrator: [seriously] Field notes end here. Whoever reads these eventually, know that certainty came slower than I expected, and considerably gentler than I feared.

quiz.question: What does the narrator identify as the actual turning point in his belief?
options: Winning a formal debate
Reading a religious text for the first time
A conversation with a colleague
Admitting he'd been rigging his own doubt whenever obedience grew inconvenient
quiz.explanation: He says the turning point wasn't a debate he won, but admitting his doubt conveniently arrived whenever obedience was inconvenient.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say about his prior skepticism upon reflection?
options: It was purely rational and consistent
It never actually existed
It was remarkably selective, dressed up as intellectual rigor
It was shared by all his colleagues equally
quiz.explanation: He admits his skepticism was 'remarkably selective' rather than the consistent rigor he'd credited himself with.

quiz.question: What comparison does the narrator draw between scientific experiments and faith?
options: They have nothing in common
Experiments are more reliable than any belief
Experiments rest on unprovable assumptions trusted provisionally, similar to larger claims he now trusts
Faith requires no trust at all
quiz.explanation: He notes that every experiment rests on assumptions he cannot ultimately prove, only trust provisionally, paralleling his trust in larger claims.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say tauhid actually asked of him?
options: To abandon all inquiry and questioning
To stop working as a researcher
To reject scientific methodology entirely
To admit inquiry has a ceiling he'd mistaken for a wall
quiz.explanation: He states tauhid didn't demand abandoning inquiry, only humility about inquiry's ceiling, which he'd mistaken for an impassable wall.

quiz.question: How does the narrator describe his mother's understanding compared to his own?
options: She understood far less than he did
She arrived at conclusions it took him a doctorate and stubbornness to approach sideways
She never discussed belief with him
Her education exceeded his own
quiz.explanation: He notes his mother, without formal education, reached conclusions that took him a doctorate and considerable stubbornness to approach.

quiz.question: Why does the narrator distrust his former skepticism?
options: It appeared most strongly when obedience became inconvenient.
It lacked scientific vocabulary.
His colleagues had rejected it.
It made experiments impossible.
quiz.explanation: He notices that his doubt was selective and conveniently timed.

quiz.question: What point does he make about scientific practice?
options: It also relies on assumptions trusted provisionally.
It can prove every assumption.
It has no place in faith.
It should replace all metaphysical questions.
quiz.explanation: He compares scientific assumptions with the provisional trust present in other serious claims.

quiz.question: Why does he call this comparison “not a knockdown argument”?
options: He refuses to present a limit of inquiry as a simplistic proof.
He thinks empirical work is useless.
He has abandoned faith.
He wants to avoid all conclusions.
quiz.explanation: The narrator carefully limits what the comparison can establish.

quiz.question: How does faith alter his approach to research?
options: He stops testing claims.
He keeps the same rigor while seeing a wider authorship.
He accepts weak methods.
He abandons professional standards.
quiz.explanation: He explicitly says he will continue rigorous experiments and reject poor methodology.

quiz.question: What does the closing tone suggest about his change?
options: It arrived suddenly through a public victory.
It developed slowly and felt gentler than expected.
It removed every question at once.
It depended on his mother’s formal education.
quiz.explanation: He describes certainty as gradual rather than dramatic.
